name: Chichimeco
confidence_why: Kelterer 2017 (first-hand acoustic fieldwork), Arellanes et al. 2011 and Herrera Zendejas 2009 (known through Lizárraga 2018's summary) all place non-contrastive stress on the stem syllable, the second syllable of the obligatory prefix+stem content word, and differ only in how they word the rule for the rare longer words ('last syllable' vs 'root syllable'), a point Lizárraga 2018 leaves open.

catalog_quote: Word structure. In Chichimeco, only function words such as sáɁ 'already' and ki 'and' are monosyllabic. Content words, on the other hand, by all accounts have to consist of a stem and a prefix and are bisyllabic (cf. Romero 1957-1958, cf. examples in Herrera 2014). ... In the vast majority of words, the prefix and the stem correspond to one syllable each, such as in (2.15) and (2.18). In some words, however, part of the stem is syllabified into the first syllable and suffixes can be included in the second syllable, such as in (2.16). The second syllable in such words, i.e. the stem syllable, is always stressed. This means that the vowel has a longer duration and a higher intensity (Herrera 2014). Most importantly for this thesis, breathy vowels seem to occur only in the stressed stem syllable (cf. Herrera 2014, Romero 1957-1958; see Section 2.3.2.). ... [p. 20:] Apart from suffixes like -k' '2OBJ' that are syllabified with the stressed stem syllable, there are suffixes that expand the word by a syllable. This affixation results in a three-syllable word, e.g. (2.17) and (2.18). Three-syllable words also result from compounding, e.g. (2.19). Suffixes can also concatenate and result in four-syllable words, e.g. (2.20). In sum, only more morphological complexity than the 'minimal' word, i.e. prefix + stem, can lead to words with more than two syllables. ... [p. 33:] creaky voice quality only occurs in the second syllable of these words, i.e. the stressed stem syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the stem (root) syllable. Every content word is minimally a monosyllabic prefix plus a monosyllabic stem, so in the minimal word stress is on the second (= final) syllable; when suffixes or compounding add syllables (three- and four-syllable words such as su-pã́-me, su-sa-bú-me) the stem syllable remains the stressed one. Correlates: longer vowel and higher intensity (attributed to Herrera 2014); glottal consonants and breathy/creaky phonation are restricted to the stressed stem syllable. Stress is non-contrastive and independent of the two-tone (H/L) system; every syllable, stressed or not, bears a tone (Kelterer p. 22; Feist & Palancar 2021 sec. 3.2).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Function words (sáɁ 'already', ki 'and') are monosyllabic; connected-speech deletion can reduce a word to one syllable (ká < ikág). Lizárraga Navarro 2018 pp. 61-62, 350 reports a discrepancy in the literature: Herrera Zendejas 2009:85 locates the accent on the vowel of the LAST syllable of the word, Arellanes Arellanes et al. 2011:9 on the SECOND syllable, and she leaves open what happens in tri- and tetrasyllabic words; the same review reports that de Angulo (1933) claimed accent and vowel quantity are absent and that stress is non-contrastive (Angulo 1933, Bartholomew 1965, Herrera 2009, Arellanes et al. 2011).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (lexical/phonological word = prefix + stem [+ suffixes]); Kelterer's data are nouns in a carrier phrase and Lastra's isolation recordings from Misión de Chichimecas. The 'second/final syllable' formulations of Herrera 2009 and Arellanes et al. 2011 (second-hand via Lizárraga) coincide with the stem in the minimal disyllabic word; only Kelterer's stem-based statement covers longer words explicitly.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the single surviving variety spoken at Misión de Chichimecas, San Luis de la Paz, Guanajuato (glottocode chic1272; autonym úza'/ʔuzãʔ; ISO pei); Kelterer's 2017 fieldwork and Lastra's recordings are from that community. No dialect split is at issue.

new_statements.quote: El acento se registra como no contrastivo en el chichimeca, el ocuilteco y el matlazinca, mientras que las lenguas pames son descritas como un sistema tono-acentual, donde el acento cae en la sílaba de la raíz, en la que contrasta el tono, de manera muy similar a lo que se documenta para el otomí y el mazahua, con la diferencia de que en las primeras el prefijo puede portar acento y en las segundas no [p. 9:] En el uza' o chichimeca jonás, la palabra mínima consiste en bisílabos con prominencia en la segunda sílaba. Existen también monosílabos, aunque la mayoría de éstos son marcadores discursivos o con valor morfológico.
new_statements.translation: Stress is recorded as non-contrastive in Chichimeco, Ocuilteco and Matlatzinca, whereas the Pame languages are described as a tone-accent system in which stress falls on the root syllable, where tone contrasts, much as is documented for Otomí and Mazahua, with the difference that in the former the prefix can bear stress and in the latter it cannot. [p. 9:] In Uza' or Chichimeco Jonaz, the minimal word consists of disyllables with prominence on the second syllable. There are also monosyllables, although most of these are discourse markers or markers with morphological value.

The catalog record itself has an empty rule field (world-r2-2026-09-17), s…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress (prominence) is non-contrastive. The minimal content word is prefix + root, i.e. a disyllable with prominence on the second syllable, which is the root syllable ([σˈσ]); monosyllables (mostly discourse markers or morphological markers) carry it themselves. In prefix + disyllabic-root verb forms the paper marks the pattern σˈσσ (ex. 18c tú-'pẽhẽ 'I search'), i.e. prominence on the first root syllable, not the last syllable of the word. Tonally, Chichimeco has two level tones /A, B/ that contrast in both non-prominent and prominent syllables and in prefixes (tables 34-35), unlike Otomí/Mazahua where contour tones are confined to the prominent syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllabic words exist but are mostly discourse markers or morphological markers (p. 9). No lexical exceptions to second-syllable/root prominence are given; the paper is a lit-based tonal typology, not an instrumental stress study (data credited to Lastra 2009, Herrera 2009, Ramírez 2010, Guerrero 2011).
new_statements.identity_note: The paper's Chichimeco data are Uza' / Chichimeco Jonaz of Misión de Chichimecas, San Luis de la Paz, Guanajuato (the paper equates its 'chichimeca' with Ethnologue's 'chichimeca de Misión de Chichimecas', p. 6-7 of the genealogy section), drawing on Lastra 2009, Herrera 2009, Ramírez 2010 and Guerrero 2011. The p. 2 sentence also covers Ocuilteco, Matlatzinca and the Pame languages; the Pame 'tone-accent, stress on the root syllable, prefix may bear stress' clause is about Pame, not Chichimeco.

readall_conflicts: No contradiction among the sources on placement: Arellanes et al. 2011 (second syllable = root syllable of the prefix+root minimal word, stress non-contrastive), Kelterer 2017 (stem syllable always stressed, longer and more intense) and Herrera Zendejas 2009 as reported by Lizárraga 2018 (acento en la vocal de la última sílaba) all put prominence on the root syllable of a disyllabic content word. The only wrinkle is a difference of formulation for longer words: Herrera's 'last syllable' and Arellanes' 'second syllable / root syllable' diverge for prefix + disyllabic-root forms such as Arellanes' ex. (18c) tú-'pẽhẽ (σˈσσ, prominence on the root-initial, second syllable, not the final one); Lizárraga 2018 (p. 350) already flags the placement in 3-4-syllable words as an open question. De Angulo 1932 (per Lizárraga 2018 pp. 88-89) claimed accent and vowel length were absent; every later source supersedes that.
